2012A16.goal: Three runners on a $500$ m loop run at $4.4$, $4.8$ and $5.0$ m/s. They stop when all three are together again. Being together means each pair's distance difference is a whole number of laps.

tools.name: Relative speed
tools.fact: \text{two runners meet when }(\Delta v)\,t\text{ is a multiple of }500
tools.why: The faster one must gain whole laps.

tools.name: Common time
tools.fact: \text{all pairs meet}\iff t\text{ works for each relative speed}
tools.why: Being together means every pair coincides.

2012A16.approach: The relative speeds are $0.4$, $0.6$ and $0.2$ m/s. Each pair is together when (relative speed)$\times t$ is a multiple of $500$. Since $0.4$ and $0.6$ are multiples of $0.2$, the binding condition is $0.2t$ being a multiple of $500$.

check.q: How long until the $5.0$ and $4.8$ m/s runners first meet again?

steps.title: First common time
steps.explain: $0.2t=500k$ first at $t=2500$; then $0.4t=1000$ and $0.6t=1500$ are also multiples of $500$. So $t=2500$.

check.q: At $t=2500$, how far ahead is the fastest runner of the slowest?

2012A16.bridge: Use relative speeds and find the first time every gap is a whole number of laps.
solution: All gaps are multiples of $500$ first when $0.2t=500$, i.e. $t=2500$.
The other gaps ($1000$, $1500$) are then multiples of $500$ too.
2012A16.shortcut: Only the smallest relative speed (if the others are multiples of it) matters.
traps: Using absolute speeds and lap times ($500/4.4$ etc.).
2012A16.recognize: Runners on a loop meeting again: work with relative speeds; meetings happen when gains are whole laps.

2012A17.goal: For coprime $a>b>0$, $\tfrac{a^3-b^3}{(a-b)^3}=\tfrac{73}3$. We want $a-b$. Factor the numerator and rewrite in terms of $d=a-b$.

tools.name: Difference of cubes
tools.why: Standard factorisation.

tools.name: Rewrite in $d$
tools.why: Expand $(a-b)^2=a^2-2ab+b^2$.

tools.name: Coprimality
tools.why: A prime dividing $a-b$ and $a$ would divide $b$.

2012A17.approach: Reduce to $\tfrac{d^2+3ab}{d^2}=\tfrac{73}{3}$, i.e. $9ab=70d^2$. Since $ab$ and $d$ are coprime, $d^2$ must divide $9$. Test $d=1,3$.

check.q: Which pair has product $70$ and difference $3$?

2012A17.bridge: Rewrite as $1+\tfrac{3ab}{d^2}$ and use that $ab$ and $d$ are coprime.
2012A17.shortcut: Test the choices: $d=3$ needs $ab=70$, and $10\cdot7$ fits.
2012A17.recognize: Ratios involving $a^3-b^3$ and $(a-b)^n$: factor, rewrite $a^2+ab+b^2$ in terms of $a-b$, and use gcd arguments.

2012A18.goal: A closed curve is made of $9$ arcs of length $\tfrac{2\pi}3$, centred at vertices of a regular hexagon with side $2$. We want the enclosed area. Compare the region with the hexagon itself.

tools.name: Arc radius and angle
tools.why: Neighbouring arcs meet at side midpoints, so the radius is half the side.

tools.name: Sector area
tools.why: A third of a unit disc.

tools.name: Hexagon area
tools.why: Six equilateral triangles.

2012A18.approach: Each arc, together with its centre, bounds a $120^\circ$ sector of area $\tfrac\pi3$. In the figure, six arcs bulge outside the hexagon (adding a sector each) and three cut into it (removing a sector each). So the area is the hexagon plus a net three sectors.

steps.title: Arc size
steps.explain: Radius $1$ and angle $120^\circ$ give arc length $\tfrac{2\pi}3$ and sector area $\tfrac\pi3$.

check.q: What is the length of a $120^\circ$ arc of radius $1$?

steps.title: Add and subtract sectors
steps.explain: Starting from the hexagon ($6\sqrt3$): six outward arcs add $6\cdot\tfrac\pi3=2\pi$; three inward arcs remove $3\cdot\tfrac\pi3=\pi$. Net $+\pi$.

check.q: What is the area of a regular hexagon with side $2$?

2012A18.bridge: Start from the hexagon and add or subtract one $\tfrac\pi3$ sector per arc.
solution: Each arc has radius $1$ and angle $120^\circ$, a sector of area $\tfrac\pi3$.
Relative to the hexagon (area $6\sqrt3$), six arcs add a sector and three remove one.
2012A18.shortcut: Count outward minus inward arcs; each net arc is worth $\tfrac\pi3$.
2012A18.recognize: Curves made of circular arcs around a polygon: area = polygon $\pm$ sectors.

2012A19.goal: Paula and her helpers paint at constant rates with the same lunch break $L$ each day. Three days give three equations; we solve for $L$.

tools.name: Work = rate × time
tools.why: Lunch time is not working time.

tools.name: Testing choices
tools.why: Three equations, three unknowns; testing is fast.

2012A19.approach: Let $p$ be Paula's rate and $h$ the helpers' combined rate (houses per hour). Monday: $(8-L)(p+h)=0.5$. Tuesday: $(6.2-L)h=0.24$. Wednesday: $(11.2-L)p=0.26$. Test the choices for $L$.

steps.title: Equations
steps.explain: Monday 8:00–4:00 is $8$ h; Tuesday to 2:12 is $6.2$ h; Wednesday to 7:12 is $11.2$ h. Wednesday finishes the remaining $26\%$.

check.q: How many hours from 8:00 AM to 2:12 PM?

2012A19.bridge: Write the three daily equations and find the lunch length that makes them consistent.
2012A19.shortcut: Test choices that make $11.2-L$ and $6.2-L$ divide nicely ($10.4$ and $5.4$).
2012A19.recognize: Work-rate problems with a shared break: subtract the break from each day's hours and set up rate equations.

2012A20.goal: A random black/white $3\times3$ grid is rotated $90^\circ$; any white square that lands where a black one was becomes black. We want the probability the grid ends all black. Rotation moves squares in cycles: the centre alone, the four corners, the four edge squares.

tools.name: Cycles of the rotation
tools.why: A $90^\circ$ turn moves each corner to the next corner, and each edge square to the next edge square.

tools.name: No two adjacent whites in a 4-cycle
tools.why: A position ends black unless it and the square rotating into it were both white.

2012A20.approach: The centre must start black ($\tfrac12$). In each $4$-cycle, a position ends white only if it and its predecessor were both white, so we need no two cyclically adjacent whites. Count those patterns and multiply the three independent parts.

steps.title: The centre
steps.explain: The centre maps to itself, so it must already be black: probability $\tfrac12$.

check.q: What is the probability a given square is black?

steps.title: A 4-cycle
steps.explain: Patterns of $4$ around a cycle with no two adjacent whites: all black ($1$), one white ($4$), two opposite whites ($2$): $7$ of $16$.

check.q: How many ways to choose two non-adjacent positions on a $4$-cycle?

2012A20.bridge: Split into the centre and two $4$-cycles; require no two adjacent whites in each cycle.
solution: Each $4$-cycle needs no two cyclically adjacent whites: $\tfrac7{16}$.
2012A20.shortcut: "No two adjacent" on a $4$-cycle: the Lucas number $L_4=7$.
traps: Treating the corners and edges as one cycle of $8$.
2012A20.recognize: Rotation problems on grids: decompose into cycles of the rotation and handle each cycle independently.

2012A21.goal: $E,F,G,H$ are midpoints of $BD,AB,AC,DC$ in a tetrahedron with $A$ at the origin. They form a rectangle; we want its area. Midsegments are parallel to opposite edges and half as long.

tools.name: Midsegment theorem
tools.fact: EF\parallel AD,\ EF=\tfrac12AD;\quad FG\parallel BC,\ FG=\tfrac12BC
tools.why: In triangles $ABD$ and $ABC$.

tools.name: Perpendicular edges
tools.why: $AD$ is along the $z$-axis and $BC$ lies in the $xy$-plane.

2012A21.approach: $EFGH$ has sides parallel to $AD$ and $BC$, each half as long. Since $AD\perp BC$, it is a rectangle with sides $\tfrac32$ and $\tfrac{\sqrt5}{2}$.

check.q: What is the distance from $(1,0,0)$ to $(0,2,0)$?

2012A21.bridge: Use midsegments: sides are half of $AD$ and half of $BC$.
2012A21.shortcut: Midpoints of four edges of a tetrahedron always form a parallelogram with sides half of the two remaining edges.
traps: Computing all coordinates when midsegments suffice.
2012A21.recognize: Midpoints of tetrahedron edges: midsegment theorem in the faces.

2012A22.goal: $1+3+\cdots$ ($m$ terms) exceeds $2+4+\cdots$ ($n$ terms) by $212$. We sum all possible $n$. Both sums have closed forms, and completing squares gives a factoring.

tools.name: Odd and even sums
tools.why: Standard formulas.

tools.name: Completing the square
tools.why: Make a perfect square.

tools.name: Difference of squares
tools.why: Factor.

2012A22.approach: $m^2-n(n+1)=212$. Multiply by $4$ and complete the square: $(2m)^2-(2n+1)^2=847=7\cdot11^2$. Factor pairs give $(m,n)$.
2012A22.bridge: Use the sum formulas, complete the square, and factor $847$.
2012A22.shortcut: Multiplying by $4$ to complete the square is the standard move for $n(n+1)$.
2012A22.recognize: Equations like $m^2-n(n+1)=k$: complete squares and factor a difference of squares.

2012A23.goal: Six people, each with the same number of friends among the group, not nobody and not everybody. We count such friendship networks: labelled regular graphs on $6$ vertices of degree $1,2,3,4$.

tools.name: Complements
tools.why: Swapping friends and non-friends.

tools.name: Perfect matchings
tools.why: Pair the first person ($5$ ways), the next unpaired ($3$), the last ($1$).

tools.name: 2-regular graphs
tools.why: Each person has two friends, so the graph is a union of cycles.

2012A23.approach: Degree $1$ graphs are perfect matchings; degree $4$ are their complements. Degree $2$ graphs are unions of cycles (a hexagon or two triangles); degree $3$ are their complements. Add.

steps.title: Degree 1 and 4
steps.explain: Perfect matchings: $15$. Complements give degree $4$: another $15$.

check.q: How many perfect matchings on $4$ people?

steps.title: Degree 2 and 3
steps.explain: A $6$-cycle: $\tfrac{5!}{2}=60$. Two triangles: $\tfrac12\binom63=10$. Total $70$; complements give $70$ more.

check.q: How many ways to split $6$ people into two groups of $3$?

2012A23.bridge: Count regular friendship graphs by degree, using complements.
2012A23.recognize: "Everyone has the same number of friends": count regular graphs; use complements and cycle structures.

2012A24.goal: Two quadratic equations in $a\ge b\ge c$ are given. Adding them gives a sum of squared differences, which pins down the gaps between $a,b,c$. Then one equation finds $a$.

tools.name: Sum of squared differences
tools.why: Expand the right side.

tools.name: Small integer solutions
tools.why: Check small nonnegative values.

2012A24.approach: Add the equations: $(a-b)^2+(b-c)^2+(c-a)^2=14$. With gaps $x=a-b$, $y=b-c$: $x^2+xy+y^2=7$. Try both gap pairs in the first equation.

steps.title: Add the equations
steps.explain: Adding: $2a^2+2b^2+2c^2-2ab-2bc-2ca=14$, so the three squared differences sum to $14$, i.e. $x^2+y^2+(x+y)^2=14$, or $x^2+xy+y^2=7$.

2012A24.bridge: Add the equations to get the gaps, then substitute into the first equation.
2012A24.shortcut: When two messy equations have coefficients that sum nicely, add (or subtract) them first.
traps: Forgetting to check both gap orders.
2012A24.recognize: Symmetric quadratic forms: look for combinations that become sums of squares.

2012A25.goal: Three random reals in $[0,n]$; we want the smallest $n$ with $P(\text{all pairwise gaps}\ge1)>\tfrac12$. The "spread out" region has a neat volume formula.

tools.name: Gap transformation
tools.why: Sort the numbers; subtracting $0,1,2$ from them maps the valid region onto a cube-like region of side $n-2$, scaling volume by $(n-2)^3/n^3$.

2012A25.approach: Use $P=\left(1-\tfrac2n\right)^3$ and solve $\left(1-\tfrac2n\right)^3>\tfrac12$. Check the boundary values.

steps.title: The probability
steps.explain: For sorted $x<y<z$ with gaps at least $1$, set $y'=y-1$, $z'=z-2$: then $x\le y'\le z'$ in $[0,n-2]$. Volume ratio $\tfrac{(n-2)^3}{n^3}$.

2012A25.bridge: Use $P=(1-\tfrac2n)^3$ and test values near the cube-root bound.
2012A25.recognize: "No two within distance $d$" for random points on an interval: shift sorted values to get $\left(\tfrac{n-(k-1)d}{n}\right)^k$.
